en: The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baoyun Shouduan, Volume One, Part One.
The Dharma Talks from the Ascending the Hall have already been included in the third volume of the *Continued Publication of the Essential Sayings of Ancient Venerable Masters*. Therefore...
I shall not record this again; I have merely collected what was omitted.
[In the *Platform Sutra*, Huineng says: "To offer this profound mind to the lands of all dust-motes—this is called repaying the Buddha's kindness. Yuancong, however, was not like this:
"At times he would pick wild vegetables and boil them with their roots; he would chop fresh firewood and burn it with its leaves."
Addressing the assembly, he said: "When I press my finger, the Ocean-Seal emits light. Holding up his staff, he said:

"Mountains, rivers, the great earth, waterfowl, and forest trees—sentient and insentient beings alike—all issue forth a great lion’s roar from the tip of this staff, expounding the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
But tell me, what Dharma-gate do Tiantai and Nanyue preach? Nanyue preaches the Dong [shan]."
The five ranks of mountain practice: ruler and subject, father and son, each attaining their proper place. Do not linger at the cold crags where strange grasses grow green;

to sit and cut off the white clouds, the lineage will not flourish. Tiantai speaks of Linji’s Three Mysteries and Three Essentials, the Four Kinds of Discernment, and how a single shout distinguishes guest and host.
When illumination and function operate simultaneously, if you wish to understand the meaning within this, it is like striking the third watch at midday. Mount Lu...
Shan came out and said: "You two fellows are right in the midst of a tangle of vines. Have you not heard it said:
'If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata'?
If the insights of these three men were weighed on the scale of a true monk, one would weigh eight *liang*, another half a *jin*, and the third would not even be worth half a *jin*.
A copper coin. Now tell me: which of these is not worth even half a coin? I only wish that the spring breeze would exert its full strength and blow them all at once into my gate.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, universally manifesting before all sentient beings. Responding to conditions as they arise, there is nowhere it does not reach;
yet it ever remains upon this seat of Bodhi. Great assembly, how do you explain the principle of responding to conditions as they arise?
In the mere space of a single snap of the fingers, the capacities and karmic roots of all living beings throughout the entire world—[all at once...]"

It should be complete and sufficient, yet not a single hair’s breadth has ever been moved. This may be called responding to conditions and meeting with stimuli while constantly remaining in this seat.
Just as I, this mountain monk, have accepted the invitation for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly and am about to take my leave of the great assembly to go to Susong County;
only after opening the hall there will I return to the monastery. Now tell me: have I left this seat?
There is none. If you say they are separate, that is merely the proliferation of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). If you say they are not separate, how do you perceive this state of non-separation?
Is it that "the realms of boundless lands are not separated from one another by so much as a hair’s tip, and the ten ages of past and present do not depart from the present moment"?
Or is it that all things, being without mind, are simultaneously and spontaneously pervasive?
"Ma! If it were like that, you would be striking at the moon with a falling staff. Reaching this point, you must awaken;
after awakening, you must further encounter a person. You say: 'Once awakened, one simply stops. Why then must one further encounter a person?"

If you have attained awakening and met with others, then at the time of extending your hand in skillful means (*upāya*), there will naturally be a way for yourself to emerge at every turn, without blinding the eyes of those who study.

If you only awaken to the head of a dry radish, not only will you blind the eyes of those who study, but moreover, as soon as you move, you will first strike your own edge and wound your own hand. You should look: I, Yangqi, previously...
The Master asked, "Master Weng Ciming said: 'The dark birds chirp and chatter; leaving the clouds, they enter the tangled peaks.
What does this mean? He replied, "I walk through the wild weeds; you, too, have entered a deep village. [The student] pressed further, saying, "An official allows not even a needle to pass;
let me ask one more question. Master Weng then gave a shout. [The student] said, "A fine shout! Master Weng shouted again. My late teacher also shouted. Master Weng—
He then gave two consecutive shouts. The former master then performed a prostration. The assembly must understand this:
those who have attained awakening and encounter others may meet them at a crossroads, yet clasp hands atop a thousand peaks;
they may meet atop a thousand peaks, yet clasp hands at a crossroads. Therefore, I, this mountain monk, have often composed a verse concerning him: He...
Where others dwell, I do not dwell; where others walk, I do not walk. It is not that it is difficult for me to dwell together with others;
rather, it is that the distinction between the monastic and the lay must be clearly maintained.
Now, as this mountain monk departs, I have untied the mouth of my sack and scattered its contents all at once before you. Those who have eyes, do not mistake this for something else. Take care.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The clay Buddha does not cross water; the wooden Buddha does not cross fire; the golden Buddha does not enter the furnace;
the true Buddha sits within. "Great assembly! This old man Zhaozhou has twelve joints of bone and eighty-four thousand pores."
At one time, I cast it all into the laps of everyone present. Today, Yuantong, seeing injustice on the road, speaks out on behalf of the ancients.

Striking the meditation seat with his hand, he said: "One must know that the seas and mountains submit to the enlightened sovereign; one cannot believe that Heaven and Earth would trap a virtuous man."
The Master’s surname was Ge; he was a native of Hengyang. In his youth, he devoted himself to calligraphy and literature.

Upon reaching adulthood, he followed Chan Master Yu of Chaling for tonsure and ordination, then traveled to study under Yangqi. One day, Yangqi suddenly asked him, “Who is your preceptor? The Master replied, “Chan Master Yu of Chaling.
Yangqi said, “I have heard that upon falling over a bridge, he attained realization and composed a most extraordinary verse. Can you remember it?”
The Master recited: "I have a single bright pearl; for a long time it has been locked away by the dust of worldly toil.

Today, the dust is cleared and its light shines forth, piercing through the myriad peaks of mountains and rivers. Daofu laughed and hurriedly rose. The Master was startled and could not sleep all night.
At dawn, he questioned him about this. It happened to be the end of the year. Daofu said, "Did you see those performing the *daguana* exorcism yesterday? He replied, "I saw them."
Qí said, "In every respect, you fall short of him. The Master was again startled and asked, "What is the meaning of this?
Qí replied, "He loves being laughed at; you fear being laughed at. The Master attained great enlightenment. He served as an attendant for a long time before taking leave to travel to Mount Lú.

Cíyuán Tóngnè Císhī appointed him to preside over Chéngtiān Monastery, where his reputation became widely renowned. Later, he yielded the position to another to reside at Yuántong, and subsequently moved to Fǎhuá and Longmén.
Master Xinghua Haihui gathered a multitude wherever he went, like clouds assembling. A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master said, "Pressing a gourd underwater. Another monk asked, "Not seeking the various sages and not esteeming one's own spiritual nature is still not the business of a patch-robed monk.
What, then, is the business of a patch-robed monk? The Master said, "Dead water does not harbor dragons."

[The monk] asked, "If one goes directly like this, what then? The Master said, "You will be utterly deceived. In the fifth year of the Xīnǐng era of Emperor Rénzōng of the Song dynasty, the year of Bǐngxū, he passed away.
His worldly age was forty-eight.
Praise for Master Yangqi: A pearl in the azure sea;
piercing through the thick mud. The tiger roars and the dragon sighs; the cock crows and the dog barks. Throughout the world, there is only Yangqi.
How truly extraordinary!
The metaphor of the "Water-Moon" used by my preceptor at Chaling in Hengzhou has been common since ancient times; yet I am not like that—what is it that I now set forth? A hundred-foot [pole]...
Having once advanced to the tip of the staff, one step upon the mountain stream bridge submerges the rivers and mountains. It is certainly not a journey; what journey could there be?
Xuan Sha and Baoshou—how they were like a pair of companions! To the east of Yanfeng, at the mouth of the Mi River, for thirty-three autumns he let out the great lion’s roar.
Unfolding and rolling up, it is all finished; as before, the Mi River flows empty.
The waters of the rivers flow; the nine tributaries lie thousands of li apart. The father has heavy tusks, yet the son has no teeth. In vain one tires oneself by pulling at his ears;
a single burner of incense sends forth a faint smoke that swirls, rising with the pine wind.
Inscription on the Remains Tower of Master Yunge Hui and the Towers of the Five Peaks Patriarchs:
Our patriarch occupies the center; the mountain range comes from the east in perfect alignment. The light of the stream flows away long and clear.

The monks shift the trees at the edge of the clouds; the guests offer incense by the seashore. From this point on, along the banks of the Xiao and Xiang rivers, the lingering influence shall resound through Luoyang.
*The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baoyun Shouduan*, Volume Upper.
*The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Baoyun Shouduan*, Volume Lower.
In the Verse on the Ancient Case:
One day the World-Honored One ascended the seat. As soon as the assembly had gathered and settled, Mañjuśrī struck the gavel and said, "Contemplate clearly the Dharma of the Dharma-King;
the Dharma of the Dharma-King is thus. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat.
The towering form of the crown-marks is ultimately difficult to behold; its unfolding and rolling back are like a flash of lightning.
Had there been people of this present age at that time, Mañjuśrī would have distinguished the needlework beneath his hammer.
“World-Honored One, when an outsider asked, ‘I do not ask about having words; I do not ask about being without words,’ the World-Honored One remained seated.
The outsider praised him, saying, ‘The World-Honored One, with great kindness and great compassion, has cleared away my clouds of delusion and enabled me to enter.
He then paid homage and departed. Later, Ānanda asked the Buddha, ‘What did that outsider realize that he said he had entered?’”
The Honored One said: Like a fine horse of the world that moves at the mere sight of the whip’s shadow;
ten-thousand-foot deep cold pools are clear to their very bottom. When the night is still, the scaled dragon moves toward the light; cast with the pole in a single throw, it follows the hook upward.
Across the vast expanse of the water, the moonlight disperses its brilliance.
When Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty invited Master Fu to lecture on the sutras, the Master ascended the seat, struck the lectern once with a ruler, and immediately descended.
The Emperor was astonished. Master Zhi asked, "Does Your Majesty understand? The Emperor said, "I do not understand.
Zhi replied, "The Master’s lecture on the sutras is finished."
When did the Great Being ever understand how to lecture on the sutras? Master Zhigong used skillful means to assist him. With a single sweep of his hand, everything on the desk was removed;
this left King Liang staring with eyes bulging. But tell me, what was it that caused those eyes to bulge?
The Baguā Monk (Pú-dài Héshàng) was often on the main thoroughfares. Someone asked him, "What are you doing here? The Master said, "I am waiting for someone to come.
The man said, "He has arrived! The Master replied, "You are not that person. At other times, he would untie his cloth bag, which contained all manner of objects.
He would scatter them down and say, "Look! Look! Then, picking each one up one by one, he would ask people, "What is this called?"
Or, while reaching for fruit from within his bag to give to a monk, as the monk was about to receive it, the Master withdrew his hand and said, "You are not that person.
Or, seeing a monk pass by, he struck him on the back once; when the monk turned his head, the Master said:

"Bring me a coin. At times he would lean against his sack and sleep soundly all day long; at other times he would rise and wander through the marketplaces, where children would clamor and chase after him.
Sometimes he would play with the children using a staff or a rosary. Once, a monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
He then dropped his sack, stood with his hands folded in *añjali*, and the monk said, "Just this."
There is nothing else besides this. The Master picked up his cloth bag, slung it over his shoulder, and departed.
It is but a single cloth bag; what marvel could one seek within? When weary, it serves as a pillow; carrying it along causes no hindrance.
Sometimes he opens it in the bustling marketplace, yet for the most part, it is his own goods for sale.
In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Buddha told Ānanda: "When I do not see, how can you not see the place where I do not see?

If you were able to see my non-seeing, it would naturally not be that characteristic of non-seeing. If you cannot see the ground of my non-seeing, it is naturally not a material object; how then could it not be you?"
The pillar before the hall has long been pregnant; the child born is truly most talented. Before he can speak, he composes a rhapsody;
with a single stroke, he wins the honor of top scholar.
In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Buddha said to Ānanda: "If one can transform objects, one is identical to the Tathāgata;

if one can transform objects, one is the Tathāgata. When spring arrives and mountain flowers bloom everywhere, there is naturally a pair of hands for the destitute that have never easily performed the *Santai* dance.
In the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, thirty-two bodhisattvas each expounded the gate of non-duality. When it came to Vimalakīrti, he remained silent.
Mañjuśrī praised him, saying: "To be without even words or letters—this is the true entry into the gate of non-duality."
One, two, hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions—counting on one's fingers to seek out the characters, one cannot keep track. For a moment, leave them before the dark window;
tomorrow, I shall calculate them with you again.
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra speaks of entering nirvāṇa without severing afflictions.
Born in the morning and dying by evening—countless millions of times. How many times in a single day do they meet face-to-face? When the battle lines are drawn and the banners unfurled, they emerge;
when a single finger moves, the guest sees the play.

*Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "If a person is treated with contempt by others, it is because that person’s karmic offenses from previous lives ought to have caused them to fall into the evil realms;
however, because they are now treated with contempt by people in this life, their karmic offenses from previous lives are thereby extinguished, and they shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Who does not know that water does not wash water? The whirlwind is eternally still, yet it rushes about incessantly.
If one could calculate the days of a thousand years, one might avoid being pushed from the palm of the patrol officer.
When the World-Honored One was at the assembly on Vulture Peak, he held up a single flower and, with his blue-lotus eyes, showed it universally to the great multitude.
Among the hundreds of thousands of sages and worthies, only Kāśyapa broke into a slight smile.

The World-Honored One said, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, the reality-phenomenon that is formless—the subtle and wonderful Dharma-gate. I entrust this to you. You...
You should protect and propagate this, lest it be severed.
To say that the entire matter is exhausted in the picking of the flower and the subtle smile is not to know how to employ the fundamental style of the school.
If one claims that the mind and the eyes are realized simultaneously, one cannot avoid remaining dimly aware within a dream.
Kāśyapa, prompted by Ānanda’s question—“Beyond the transmission of the golden robe, what else does the World-Honored One transmit?”—called out to Ānanda.
Ānanda responded with “Yes. Kāśyapa said, “Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate.”
Beyond the golden brocade robe, what else remains to be transmitted? When the younger brother responds to the elder’s call, how could there be partiality?
If one were to overturn the banner-pole before the gate, one would avoid having it continue to lean against the wall as before.
When Master Bodhidharma met Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, the Emperor asked, "What is the primary meaning of the holy truths?
The Master replied, "Vast emptiness; there is no sage. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that stands before me? The Master said, "I do not know. The Emperor did not awaken.
The Master then broke off a reed and crossed the river to reach Wei. Later, when the Emperor raised the matter and questioned Master Zhi, the Master said, "Does Your Majesty recognize this man?
The Emperor replied, "I do not. The Master said, "This is the Great Being Avalokiteśvara; he transmits the Buddha’s Mind-Seal."

The Emperor said, "I shall dispatch an envoy to issue an imperial decree to him. The Master said, "Do not speak of Your Majesty’s decree; even if everyone in the entire kingdom were to go, he would still not return.
A single arrow usually brings down a single vulture; having already spared him with an extra arrow, let him return directly to the peak of Shaoshi."
He sat. Emperor Xiao of the Liang dynasty ceased speaking and departed to summon him again.
Bodhidharma traveled from Liang to Wei and reached Shaolin Temple in Luoyang, where he sat facing a wall for nine years.
Having already been exposed by King Liang, he sat alone at Shaolin; in vain did he speak of a "special transmission outside the teachings," for how could he fail to recognize this very thing?
When the Second Patriarch, Master Huike, first visited Bodhidharma, he stood in the snow and cut off his arm, saying, "My mind is not yet at peace."
The Master requested Mazu to settle his mind. Mazu said, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall settle it for you. The Master replied, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable.
Mazu said, "I have finished settling your mind for you. At this, the Master attained awakening.
Searching from beginning to end for the mind, nothing can be found; in vast stillness, not a trace of the Shaolin man is seen. The old snow fills the courtyard, its chill known once more;
the nostrils remain, as ever, tucked above the upper lip.
The Great Master Wuzu Hongren was, in a previous life, planting pine trees on the western mountains of Qizhou when he encountered the Fourth Patriarch, who told him:
"I wish to transmit the Dharma to you, but you are already advanced in years. If you were to come again, I would still be waiting for you."
The Master agreed. He subsequently went to the Zhou family, where he took birth as a daughter. Because she was cast into a muddy stream, she was protected by a divine being.

When she reached the age of seven, she became a young boy. One day, while traveling to Huangmei, the Patriarch encountered a small child whose physical features were remarkably distinguished and elegant.
The Master then asked, "What is your surname? He replied, "I have a surname, but it is not an ordinary surname. The Master asked, "What is this surname? He replied, "It is Buddha-nature.
The Master asked, "Do you have no nature? He replied, "Because nature is empty. The Master silently recognized him as a vessel for the Dharma.
He immediately had an attendant ordain him as a monk and subsequently entrusted him with his robes and bowl.

He resided at Mount Dongshan in Huangmei; his sacred authority was beyond worldly appraisal. How could the secret transmission on Double Peak be a hollow claim? His former incarnation had already grown old, making it difficult to pass on the bowl;

entrusting his shadow, he returned once more to continue the lamp. The fame of his past practice of planting pine trees still resonates today; may the myriad spirits fulfill their vow to repay his mother’s kindness.
What has increased? Today, the style of our school pervades the realm solely because, during the springtime, [Emperor] Xuanzong selected the capable Huizhong, National Teacher.
One day, the National Teacher called to his attendant; the attendant responded "Yes. He called him thus three times, and each time he responded "Yes."
The Master said: "I thought I was failing you; it turns out you are failing me.
The National Teacher called his attendant three times, and the attendant responded three times. He needlessly thrusts in needles and awls where there is no wound;
who would have known that such conduct is improper?
The State Preceptor’s Seamless Stupa:
From whose hands was this seamless stupa fashioned? Though there is a model, it cannot be transmitted; how can one insist on depicting it when it has no levels?
It shall forever hang above the crystal palace.
Chan Master Qingyuan Si was once asked by a monk, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
The Master replied, "What is the price of rice in Luling?
The price of rice in Luling is exceptionally fresh; who would discuss it without it hanging on their lips? Boundless pure breezes arise within the gate.
Externally: Do not measure intimacy by pints and pecks.
One day Mazu ascended the seat; Baizhang rolled up the mat before him, and Mazu immediately descended from the seat.
Yesterday the eastern wind was unexpectedly fierce; peach blossoms fell in confusion like a rain of red. Last night the eastern wind again went wild;
they covered the ground, yet one knows not where they have gone.
Master Mazu was unwell. The head monk asked, "How is the Master’s health these days? Mazu replied, "The Buddha of the Sun’s Face, the Buddha of the Moon’s Face.
The great earth, mountains, and rivers are all treasures; those who do not recognize them enter the wild weeds. Thus the Buddhas of the Sun’s and Moon’s Faces were revealed.
[The sun] shines forth; the light of the coral flickers brightly.
When a monk asked Zen Master Baizhang Hai, "What is the extraordinary matter? the Master said, "Sitting alone on the Great Hero Peak.
The monk bowed, and the Master struck him.
How could such great capacity and great function be in vain? Sitting alone upon the solitary peak, he possesses his own sovereign authority.
Should anyone transmit the King’s decree even slightly incorrectly, they shall receive three thousand blows upon the crown of their head.
When Zen Master Nanquan encountered two halls disputing over a cat, he addressed the assembly, saying, "If you can speak, I shall save the cat;
if you cannot speak, I shall kill it. The assembly was speechless, and the Master then killed it.
When Zhaozhou returned from outside, the Master presented him with the previous story. Zhaozhou then took off his straw sandals, placed them on his head, and walked out.
The Master said: "If you had been here just now, you would have saved the cat.
Holding up the two halls so all could see, he brandished his blade to seize the living mouser;
alas, there was no blood beneath the skin, until corpses lay strewn across the road."
The marten, in the stillness of night, stretches itself wide; extending its paw over its head, it reveals its long claws.
Having finished patrolling the old king’s chamber, it scurries out in haste, fearing the light of day.
Banshan said, "The path that goes beyond is not transmitted by the thousand sages. Ciming said, "The path that goes beyond is not so even for the thousand sages.
Yangqi said, "It is stuck on the mouth."
The path leading upward from Mount Pan—what words can describe it? Rarely is a traveler seen, for their ears have been pierced. When the mouth is brought to it, there is no place to bite;
only then does one know that the thousand sages could not transmit it.
Master Shuilao went to visit Mazu. As he rose from his prostrations, intending to pose a question, Mazu gave him a single kick that sent him tumbling to the ground.
The Master suddenly attained great enlightenment. Rising up, he laughed heartily and said, "How extraordinary! How extraordinary!
The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and immeasurable subtle meanings—all are found within a single hair-tip; one must recognize their source there."

Once it is brought down with a single step, there is cause for great laughter; all former skills and stratagems have been rendered utterly futile. Yet the serpent’s head still seeks to scratch its itch;
ten thousand, a hundred thousand, all emerge from a single hair.
When Mazu Gu was visited by the Dharma Master Liangsui, the Master shut the door and took his hoe to weed the grass.
Liangsui came again and knocked on the door. The Master asked, "Who is it? He replied, "It is I. The Master said, "You dull-witted monk, go away!
This happened three or four times in this manner. Suddenly, Liangsui had an awakening. He went back and knocked on the door, saying, "Master, do not deceive Liangsui."
Liang-sui said, "If I had not come to pay my respects to you, I would have been led astray by the twelve volumes of the scriptures for the rest of my life.
The Master then opened the door, allowing him to pass through and awakening him; he subsequently granted him formal approval (*inka*).

Liang-sui returned to the capital, where he dispersed his assembly at the lecture hall and told his disciples, "What all of you know, Liang-sui knows entirely; what Liang-sui knows, none of you know."
Shutting the door and taking up the hoe was already too late; to come back now is only to face being smeared with plaster.
Having long realized within the light that I have been deceived, I finally believe there is no one with whom I can leave the household life together.
Chan Master Baizhang Weizheng asked Nanquan, "Do the spiritual friends of all quarters have any teaching that they do not explain to people?
Nanquan replied, "There is. The Master asked, "How so? Nanquan said, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing.
The Master said, "If that is so, then you have explained it to people. Nanquan said, "I am just like this; even I..."
"Furthermore, how is it so? The Master said, "I am not even a *kalyāṇamitra* (spiritual friend); how could I know whether there is a dharma that is spoken or one that is not?
[The student] said, "I do not understand; I beg the Master to explain. The Master said, "I have already explained it to you quite thoroughly."
Nirvana is like the wind blowing past Laozi; who can know the *ra-li-li-ra*?
Across the ridges, how many people have misheard it, all at once calling it the *zhègūcí* (partridge song)?
Baizhang addressed the assembly, saying, "You all shall cultivate the fields for me, and I shall explain the Great Meaning for you.
When they had finished the communal labor of cultivating the fields, the assembly requested the Master to explain the Great Meaning. The Master simply extended both hands to show them.
I have always admired Baizhang’s unraveling of the field; it has been transmitted through the hands of practitioners from ancient times to the present. Who would say his tongue never moved?
The five notes and six pitches circulate in perfect harmony.
Luzu of Chizhou would constantly turn his back to the wall whenever he saw a monk approach. Hearing of this, Nanquan said, "I usually tell the monks:
even if one were to understand it before the Buddha appeared in the world, not even one or half of one person could be found."
He was like that for donkey-years.
Lu Zu’s solitary style shook the four quarters; when monks came, he faced the wall, known by few.
Nanquan brought up this matter of donkey-years—tell me, what time is it now?
The layman Pangyun visited Mazu and asked, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion?
Mazu replied, "Wait until you can suck up all the waters of the West River with a single draught, and then I will tell you.
At these words, the layman attained sudden enlightenment.
Sucking up the waters of the West River in a single draught—throughout ten thousand ages, not a single drop remains. One must side with principle rather than kin;
Master Ma is truly to be pitied for his narrow mouth.
Chan Master Huangbo Yun said, "You are all nothing but fellows who eat the dregs of wine. Do you know that within the Great Tang there are no Chan masters?
At that time, a monk asked, "The various quarters gather great assemblies; why do you say instead that there are no Chan masters?
The Master replied, "I do not say there is no Chan; I simply say there are no masters."
In the land of the Great Tang, there is no Chan master. Let us join hands and return home together. I cast my hook only intending to catch a fierce dragon;
who would have known I would catch this lame turtle?
Chan Master Guishan Lingyou addressed the assembly, saying: "After this old monk has passed away, I shall become a water buffalo on the mountain below.
On its left flank, I will write five characters: 'The monk so-and-so of Guishan.
If you call me the monk of Guishan, I am still the water buffalo; if you call me the water buffalo, I am still the monk of Guishan. What would you call me?"
If you say "yes," you have it;
yet I do not say it is Mount Huai, nor do I say it is the ox. Clearly, where can one discern its tracks?
To deviate by even a hair’s breadth from the path taken brings ten thousand kalpas of no possibility of emerging.
Grand Master Lu asked Nanquan, "Master Zhao is truly extraordinary; he understands that heaven and earth share a single root and all things are one body.
Nanquan pointed to a peony in the courtyard and said, "Grand Master, when people of this age see this single branch of a flower, it is as if they were dreaming."
Heaven and earth share the same root; it is naturally so. At that time, I was still joyful to have met Nanquan. He pointed and said, "Seeing these flowers is like a dream.
One must believe that within the alchemical crucible (hu) there is another heaven.

When Chan Master Longtan Chongxin had not yet left the household life, he worked at a bakery in front of Tiantai Monastery. Every day, he would regularly provide ten cakes to the Retired Emperor. After the Emperor had accepted them, he would set aside one cake and give it back to him, saying, "I bestow this upon you so that it may provide shade for your descendants. The Master replied, "This belongs to me; why do you say you are bestowing it upon me? The Emperor said: [The Emperor continued: "If you were to sell these cakes, you would have to pay taxes. Now, because I have taken them, they are no longer yours. Since they are mine, I can give them away as I please. This is why I say I am bestowing it upon you. The Master was greatly moved by these words and subsequently left home to become a monk. Later, when the Emperor visited the monastery, he asked the Master, "What did you do before you became a monk?
